questions.question: On a frontal chest radiograph, the "Oreo cookie sign" (two lucent fat lines separated by a central density) indicates:
questions.detail: The sign represents the pericardial fluid sandwiched between the epicardial and paracardial fat layers.

questions.question: What is the normal thickness of the pericardium on CT or MRI?
questions.detail: The pericardium should be thin; thickness > 3–4 mm is considered abnormal.

questions.question: Which imaging feature helps differentiate "constrictive" from "restrictive" physiology?
choices: A. Pericardial thickening/calcification and septal bounce (bounce favors constriction)
questions.detail: Septal bounce (shuddering of the septum during inspiration) is a hallmark of the mechanical tethering seen in constrictive pericarditis.

questions.question: "Congenital absence of the pericardium" most commonly involves the:
questions.detail: Left-sided absence is most common and results in leftward displacement of the heart and lung tissue interposing between the aorta and pulmonary artery.

questions.question: Pericardial calcification is a high-yield radiographic finding for:
choices: C. Chronic constrictive pericarditis (e.g., from prior TB or surgery)
questions.detail: Extensive calcification is often the sequela of old infection (TB) or inflammation and strongly suggests constriction.

questions.question: A pericardial cyst is most commonly found in which location?
questions.detail: These are typically benign, water-density cysts located at the right cardiophrenic angle.

questions.question: On MRI, "Acute Pericarditis" is best seen as:
questions.detail: Active inflammation leads to bright signal on T2 and late gadolinium enhancement of the pericardial layers.

questions.question: A "pericardial diverticulum" differs from a cyst because it:
choices: A. Communicates with the pericardial space and changes shape with position
questions.detail: Diverticula are basically cysts that maintain a connection to the main pericardial cavity.
